A change that removed an integrity check or turned a guarded update into a destructive one is the concrete gap, and it is visible in the diff to the read or write path.

boundary.title: A review, not a data-integrity platform.
boundary.paragraph: heygrc flags changes that touch the integrity safeguard and cites the CFR reference so the fix happens in the pull request. It does not hash your records or run your backups. It catches the moment a change lets ePHI be altered or destroyed without detection, at the diff.

metaDescription: Least functionality (NIST SP 800-53 CM-7) is the control that says a system should provide only essential capabilities. The shapes it takes in a pull request, a worked example of an SSH server baked into a container image, and what an assessor checks.
title: Only the capabilities you actually need.
intro: CM-7 (least functionality) is the NIST 800-53 control that says a system should be configured to provide only its essential capabilities, and to disable or restrict the services, ports, and functions it does not need. Every unnecessary capability is attack surface. And attack surface is added in code: a package installed, a service enabled, a port opened, a feature flag left on.
shapesIntro: Least functionality erodes whenever a change adds a capability the system does not need to do its job. The recurring shapes:

shapes.label: An unnecessary service is added
shapes.detail: A daemon or agent the application does not need (an SSH server, a stray sidecar) is installed and run, adding a service and a port to every instance.

shapes.label: A management or debug interface is exposed
shapes.detail: An admin console, profiler, or debug endpoint is reachable in production, giving an attacker a powerful surface to aim at.

shapes.label: A disabled port or protocol is reopened
shapes.detail: A port or an old protocol that had been turned off is enabled again for convenience, widening what can be reached.

shapes.label: A development-only feature is left on
shapes.detail: A seed route, sample data endpoint, or verbose mode meant for development ships enabled in production.

shapes.label: A broad default is left in place
shapes.detail: An insecure-but-convenient default (directory listing, a wildcard host allowlist) is left on rather than narrowed to what is needed.

example.title: An SSH server baked into a container image.
example.setup: Engineers want to shell into containers to debug, so the image installs an SSH server and starts it on boot. It works, and now every running container runs an sshd it does not need: a service listening for connections across the whole fleet, for occasional convenience.

lines.text: + RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y openssh-server
+ CMD service ssh start && python app.py

example.finding: Installing and starting an SSH server makes every container run a service it does not need, listening for connections and widening the attack surface of the whole fleet. CM-7 (least functionality) expects a system to provide only essential capabilities and to disable unnecessary services. Use the platform's exec (kubectl exec, docker exec) to get a shell when you need one, rather than baking an sshd into the image.

auditor.heading: Least functionality is checked against what is actually running.
auditor.paragraph: An assessment under NIST 800-53 looks at whether a system runs only what it needs: the services, ports, and functions that are enabled, and whether the unnecessary ones are disabled or restricted. A change that added a service, exposed a management interface, or reopened a port is the concrete expansion of attack surface behind that, and it is visible in the diff to the image, manifest, or config.

boundary.title: A review, not a hardening pipeline.
boundary.paragraph: heygrc flags changes that touch CM-7 and cites the control so the fix happens in the pull request. It does not run your benchmark scans or your hardening automation. It catches the moment a change adds a capability the system does not need, at the diff.

metaDescription: Information input validation (NIST SP 800-53 SI-10) is the control that says a system should check the validity of its inputs. The shapes it takes in a pull request, a worked example of a path-traversal from an unvalidated filename, and what an assessor checks.
title: Inputs, checked before they are trusted.
intro: SI-10 (information input validation) is the NIST 800-53 control that says a system should check the validity of the inputs it accepts. Unvalidated input is how a request gets a system to do something it should not: read a file outside its directory, call a host it should not, or process malformed data. The validation lives in the code that takes the input, and it is easy to remove without anyone noticing the consequence.
shapesIntro: Input validation weakens when a change lets untrusted input through unchecked. The recurring shapes:

shapes.label: A file path is built from unvalidated input
shapes.detail: A user-supplied name is joined into a path with no check, so a crafted value with ../ can escape the intended directory (path traversal).

shapes.label: A URL or host comes from unvalidated input
shapes.detail: A request target is taken from input without an allowlist, so the server can be made to call internal or unintended hosts (server-side request forgery).

shapes.label: A validation check is removed
shapes.detail: A check on an input's format, range, or allowed set is dropped, so malformed or hostile values now reach the logic behind it.

shapes.label: Bounds or length checks are removed
shapes.detail: Size or length limits on input are taken out, so oversized or malformed payloads get through.

shapes.label: An allowlist is replaced by accepting anything
shapes.detail: A strict allowlist of accepted values is loosened to accept arbitrary input, widening what a caller can supply.

example.title: A download path built from an unvalidated name.
example.setup: A download endpoint serves files from an upload directory by name. A change passes the user's filename straight into the path and drops the allowlist check, so a request for a crafted name escapes the directory and reads files it should not.
example.finding: Without the check, a crafted name like ../../etc/passwd escapes the upload directory (path traversal) and reads arbitrary files. SI-10 (information input validation) expects inputs to be checked for validity. Validate the name against an allowlist, or resolve the path and confirm it stays within the directory before reading.

auditor.heading: Input validation is checked where untrusted data enters.
auditor.paragraph: An assessment under NIST 800-53 looks at whether a system validates the inputs it accepts at its trust boundaries: are file names, URLs, identifiers, and payloads checked before they are used. A change that removed a validation or built a path or request from raw input is the concrete weakness behind that, and it is visible in the diff to the handler.

boundary.title: A review, not a full SAST suite.
boundary.paragraph: heygrc flags changes that touch SI-10 and cites the control so the fix happens in the pull request. It is not a replacement for your static analysis or fuzzing. It catches the moment a change lets untrusted input through unchecked, at the diff.
